title: Laying out the sheet for analysis: one row per record

videos.script: Somebody in every company keeps a spreadsheet like this one. A title across the top. The months across the columns. A subtotal under each group, and a total at the bottom. {{report}} It reads beautifully. And it cannot answer a single new question. Ask it which customer bought the most decaf, and the answer is not in it anywhere. {{question}} Here is the same business, kept another way. One row for each sale. One column for each thing we know about it. The date. The customer. The product. How many bags. {{records}} It is plainer. It is also the shape that every tool in this course reads. A formula that adds by condition. A pivot table. A query that imports and cleans. A data model with relationships. {{tools}} So this lesson does two things. First, it gets Excel ready on your own computer, because every lesson after this one asks you to type. {{lab}} Then it gives you the data. Eighteen months of sales from a small coffee roaster, Café Serra. You paste it into three sheets, and you check that it all arrived. {{paste}} And it teaches the one rule the rest depends on. One row per record. One column per field. One value in each cell. {{rule}}
